submission.natural_language_explanation: The negative pole fires on the token that supplies a time or quantity value in running text: the digits of a written year or date (1815, 1987, 1969, 1600), a calendar or clock expression that fixes when something happened (last night, next year, last October, this quarter, each month, in late August, 5 p.m.), and scale/unit words (degrees, Celsius, billion). It is keyed to the value rather than to the vocabulary, so swapping one such expression for another barely moves it (in 1815 -> in 1816: delta 0.00; last night -> last Monday: delta -0.09), while replacing it with a non-temporal phrase in the same slot drops the peak to near zero (last night -> at home: 0.24 -> 0.03; in 1987 -> in poverty: 0.27 -> 0.00), and ordinary object, place and abstract nouns in those same slots stay near zero; a few non-temporal content words (the first 'energy' of 'light energy', 'wind' of 'the cold wind') also peak and are not explained by this claim.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The dispute between the two estates concerned a boundary fence that runs along the western edge of the lower meadow. Each side produced an old map, and each map showed the fence following a shallow stream that has since shifted course. The plaintiff argued that the map held by the defendant had been altered by a previous owner, and that the alteration moved the line of the fence by the width of a cart track. The defendant answered that the alteration, whatever its origin, made no difference to the position of the stream as it appears on the ground, and that the map was offered only as a guide.

The court asked a surveyor to walk the land with the parties and to mark the line he considered consistent with the older map. The surveyor did so, and he noted that the hedgerow along the western edge had been planted by hand, row upon row, which suggested a deliberate boundary rather than a natural feature. Counsel for the plaintiff pressed him on this point, asking whether a hedgerow planted by a tenant could bind the landlord, and the surveyor, who was not a lawyer, declined to answer. The court then called a historian, who explained how boundaries of this kind were described in the old deeds.

The hearing continued in a room too small for the crowd that had gathered. The historian returned to the witness box and was taken through the deeds page by page. He agreed that the wording was ambiguous, and he agreed that copyists often shortened the descriptions they were paid to reproduce. Counsel for the defendant asked whether a shortened description could be treated as evidence of the original line, and the historian said that it could, though with caution. The judge asked him to compare the two maps himself, and he did, holding them side by side under a lamp and tracing the line of the stream with a finger.

After the evidence closed, the judge reserved judgment and asked the parties to submit written argument on the effect of the altered copy. The submissions arrived on 17 June 2019, and each side repeated the points it had made at the hearing, adding little that was new. The judge then visited the land in person, accompanied by the surveyor, and walked the line the surveyor had marked. The stream, the judge observed, had cut a new channel through the lower meadow, and the fence had been repaired with posts of different woods.

The judgment was careful. The judge held that the older map was the better evidence of the parties' intention, that the alteration did not defeat it, and that the line marked by the surveyor should be treated as the boundary. He added, however, that the defendant was entitled to compensation for the cost of the repairs he had made to the fence in reliance on the old line, and he directed that the parties agree an amount or return to the court. Neither side was content, but the litigation ended, and the fence stayed where the surveyor had put it.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A date buried deep inside a long legal narrative that is otherwise free of values, so the value-in-running-text claim predicts the date tokens still fire when the context is far longer than any scan snippet.
